evidence.text: I, I’d be much more interested if you were focused strictly on b2b. I’d love to see you doubling down on that and not the focus on direct b2c. So I think that for now, I’m a pass.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Quick question. Who’s a pet parent?

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Oh I so am.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I have a chihuahua who thinks she is my other daughter.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: I have two cats. Um, and their names are Princess Jigglypuff and Mr Polar Bear.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: That’s just silly.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: So first of all, um, I am the founder. Our CEO Krishna, my dog, and he’s at home, doing his CEO duties. And I started Spot On for him. One of the hardest things to do is getting around town with your pet without actually driving yourself. And there are Ubers and Lyfts out there and it’s very inconvenient because it’s to the discretion of the driver whether they’re going to take you or not. I had the problem because I had two big dogs. One of the biggest challenges was taking them to the airport. I’d beg my friends for rides, pay my car service $350 to go six miles. I had to, because we had a plane to catch. So step in Spot On. We’re the solution. We’re a ride hailing service for people and their pets.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: We’re actually revolutionizing pet mobility.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Hmm.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: We have unaccompanied pet rides, which we’re piloting. So if you’re a busy pet parent, you simply request a ride, we’ll take your dog, cat, hamster to a destination of your choice without you actually being there.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Can you just take us through, can you just take us through, how much are you raising and what have you raised to date and what, tell us the valuation, all that.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Sure, absolutely, yeah. We're raising $750,000. I've closed about $250,000 of that $750.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: At what valuation?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: At 3 million valuation.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Do you have a version of the app that we could see?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Yes. I do.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Yeah. That would be amazing.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: So basically you load it up on your smartphone, like so. And the map comes up, shows you drivers.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: People and cats.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: People and cats. And then you choose your drop off location, say, let’s go to Central Park Zoo. And then you choose your time.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So it’s not on-demand?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: So currently we’re not on demand. We have a 2-hour booking window. And that’s because we have to get enough drivers on our platform in order to be on demand.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: You have a two hour booking window?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Wow.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That’s a problem.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: It actually hasn’t been a problem. Because a lot of people schedule their animal’s visits, they know when they’re going to work.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That’s true. No, that’s true. That's true.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: But when we do go on-demand we’re still going to have this booking option, because everybody seems to like it. Our drivers like it too.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So tell me a little about you, could you please? And your team.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Sure. We’re a team of four. Um, I’m the founder and CEO. And ah the last company that I started a boutique marketing firm. Ran that for 12 years. My CTO and co-founder John, when I told him about this, um, idea he was like, you wanna do what? It’s like, like Uber for pets. And then ah three months later he calls me back and he was like, I’ve been an Uber driver for three months. I kinda figured this out, I think we can do it, and we can do it better. So that’s the kind of team I have.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Huh!

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Wow.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: We, and actually we did a pilot in LA. And I printed up some flyers, went to the dog park. We started getting calls. Hey, can you come pick us up? Sure! I was driver number one. We took over 500 rides. My friends were driving for me. Um and that's why I knew I had something.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Wow.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I like your moxie.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: And, and actually to go even further, I stood outside LAX, talked to every dog, cat person that was coming in. Asked them, How did you get here? Do you have any idea if there's a convenient solution? And I put all this together, and now we have Spot On, that's humming here in New York City.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: First of all, I am so impressed by you.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Oh thank you.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I just have to say.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Give us an example of a ride and how much money do you get paid.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Like let's say, let's say it's someone from downtown Manhattan to one of the airports and they did it in an Uber. What would they pay then? What would they pay with you? What's your cut?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Yeah, absolutely. So we're actually the most profitable ride hailing company in New York City. Our rides are very similar to your Uber and Lyft but we are a little bit more expensive because we're a premium service.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: So we, we're more in the Uber Black range as far as what you would pay to be in one of our cars. Average ride is about $35. We take 15% of that fare. And then the remaining 85% is given to the driver. So that's kind of where the breakdown is.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You realize that Uber and Lyft are more like 20, 25%?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Exactly. We actually give our drivers more of an incentive to take pets. With Uber and Lyft, they're not going to take you. But because we're offering that financial incentive.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Why do you say they're not gonna take you? I've been in those a ton of times with animals.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: No, you're right, you're right. There are drivers out there that will. It's just a hit or miss. Ours is a guaranteed service.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: But don't you just get into an Uber and hand the guy $20 or $50 extra and he'll just say, Okay, I'll take it.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I, I, I was not aware that they have the right to turn you down if you have a pet.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Absolutely. We've actually been getting a lot of reports.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: If you have an allergy, yes, but.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Exactly. That's the exact reason why.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Doesn't money solve that problem?

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Some people are.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Michael, money doesn’t solve all problems. You can’t just hand 20 bucks to someone.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: For, for Uber drivers with a dog it does.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Wouldn’t it also be easy for Uber to have a pet option in their app? And just say, you know.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Yeah, that's what I'm thinking. Like, can't you just have like a feature in the settings? It’s like, turn it on.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Pet friendly.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: To, to answer that question, Uber has recently added Uber Pets. They relaunched it for the fourth time. It's not available in New York City. Ah, they've ah launched it 2013 in Dallas, 2015 in Turkey, 2017 in Singapore. And now 2019, every two years, ah they've expanded it to Austin, Philly.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: But seeing your success...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How is that...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: ...don't you think Uber would then see this as natural? Because you've already primed the pump, so to speak.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Right, the issue with how Uber is doing it is that they're basically taking the existing human formula and laying it on top of a pet formula. So what we're seeing coming out of Austin, Philadelphia, and the markets that they're in now, Nashville, is that yeah, they're clicking Uber Pet. Drivers aren't available. Drivers keep canceling. It's not a guaranteed service. They're still not finding that.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Does it strike anybody that Uber and Lyft struggle?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: To do this?

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: No! To make any money!

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Yes, of course.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So I, I, I guess what I'm struggling at, if you're 35 bucks a ride, that's what you said, and you get a 15%, I don't know, 5 bucks to you.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And what does that represent in revenues?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Revenue wise? Close to about $112,000 a month.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: In?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: In gross.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: In gross.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So you're 15% of that.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: We're 15% of that.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Yeah. Can you move that 15% to 25?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: We are.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Can you make more money?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Yes. This is our testing phase.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I was just going to say, like, Uber X is a tough business. Uber Black is not a tough business.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Correct.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: And so if you're doing Uber Black pricing, you can avoid the bottom-feeding pricing competition…

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: That's a good point. That's, that's a good response.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: ... behavior that drags down margins in more price-sensitive.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: And we also have a specific clientele that we're going after.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I'm liking it again a bit more now.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: And we have a specific clientele that we’re going after.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: What's your customer acquisition cost? If you make 5 bucks?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: So currently our customer acquisition costs are under a dollar.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Hm.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: I'll tell you why. It's our B2B strategy. We've partnered up with several partners. They're bringing in over 65% of our rides, which is lowering our cost of customer acquisition.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Who's that?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Google. WeWork. Petco. Many vets in the city. Google and WeWork, we're servicing their pet-friendly office spaces. So you would get a discount on our rides for being an employee at Google.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: My question was going to be what percentage of this is repeat usage? Because like this feels to me the kind of business where if you find, if you tap into those people, it becomes a habit.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Right. I mean, right now, our usage, our repeat usage is close to I'd say 45%. Once they use us once, they're hooked, because they know that we have a service that is not just guaranteed but we're safe. Our drivers are amazing.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Trust.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Trust.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You've built trust.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Tell us, how does this become a big business. I'm struggling because I like you, I like the pitch. I love what Charles had to say, which kind of got me off of the Uber X and on to the Uber Blacks. And now I'm thinking, how does it become not a niche-y business, how is this a business business?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: If you look at the pet landscape, there's nobody that's in pet mobility right now. We can harness the power of a pet market by groomers and daycares. How many day carers are there here in New York City?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh, a gazillion.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: So we can essentially become their transportation service.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Have you talked to them?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: We are currently talking to them, and that's why I said our partnership with Petco is actually going to really, um, take this to another level.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I'm sorry, what is the deal with Petco? What, what are they doing for you?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: So we're basically going to be servicing their Union Square location. So bringing pets to and from Union Square, with or without their owners, depending on what kind of, if they're going for a grooming, or otherwise.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Can we reframe that a little bit, though. Like it sounds to me like you have a couple of different services. You have, like Michael said, you have the like, it's you and your dog going across town.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Maybe Uber can do that easily.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: But then you've got the unaccompanied pet going to the vet.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: There it's like a training.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: typical ride-share....

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: That's a cool service by the way.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So what, what, what percentage of rides are these unaccompanied?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: They just started it.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: So we're just piloting that with our vet partners. Um, so what we've been seeing is probably about, ah, close to about 150 coming in a month. And it's very limited because we want to make sure we perfect it before we, ah, release it to the public.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How many vet partners do you have?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: We have over 20 in New York City.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: First of all, I am squarely in your target market. Like, I pay a vet to come to my house. I live in Boston. And I have two cats who hate to be in the car. I would pay so much just for the peace of mind, like, if I can’t be there on the unaccompanied visit, that’s a skill. Imagine like a baby carrier installation.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: The unaccompanied visits are different.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: But aren’t you the edge case? Like everything you just said there...

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Well, that's what I'm struggling with is...

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: She's not common. Who has a vet coming to their home?

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: But no, like literally, the vet, that vet is completely booked out forever. She is so, they’re so highly in demand.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Okay, so what do you think of this business?

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: I really like it.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I do too.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: I think I'm gonna invest.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Me too.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Thank you guys.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I really like the business too. Um, I am not gonna invest yet. Something Michael said I think we need to run down and I don’t think we can do it in this room. Which is, let’s assume that the, Hey, I’m just going from Central Park back to my house with my pet after a fun day out, assuming that business gets commoditized, is the remainder of the business interesting? It might turn out that, like, for the accompanied pet visit, you could charge way more.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Way more.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: So I’m going to pass for now. But I would like to spend time with you and see if I could get convinced that assuming that that business gets commoditized, or at a minimum gets more competitive, what models could you use on the higher end things that are more difficult to replicate? And does that yield an interesting company? I think, and my hunch is the answer is probably it does.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: What’s the biggest thing you need to do with this product?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: The biggest thing we need to do is expand our footprint in New York City and show the scalability.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: How do you do that?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: In order for us to do that, we need to really pump more money into our marketing. What we’ve been doing right now is relying heavily on our business partners, which is great. But there are a lot of people out there that don’t know about us, and we really need to...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So you’re not, you’re not focused then 100% on the b2b? You want to expand the b2c marketing channel?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Well, we are a b2c business, at the end of the day. Right. It’s just...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: It’s a b2b2c.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. It’s just how we acquire our customers. So absolutely we want to expand the b2b. But in order for us to really show the full width and breadth of what we do, we really need to get the customer directly.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I, I’d be much more interested if you were focused strictly on b2b. I’d love to see you doubling down on that and not the focus on direct b2c. So I think that for now, I’m a pass.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Why did you call the company Spot On? It sounds like they're a carpet cleaning. Like, why not, Pet Ride?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: That would be Spot Off.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: You know, like Pet Ride. Why wouldn't it be Pet Ride? Like what you do.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay, no, no, you're spot on. Because that is actually...

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Thank you Jillian.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: ...what I was thinking too. Spot On, I have zero. It's easy to spell, easy to remember. But what does it have to do with, with the service?

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: So Spot is a common name for a dog, cat. And...

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Not a cat. There's no cats named Spot!

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I don't think anyone names their dog Spot either.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: But okay, so Spot...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: We digress.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Would you be open to rebranding this, so that it has...

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Pet Ride.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: ...more of, Pet... something that, that people would associate.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Yeah. I mean, we're, we're, we're new enough that we can.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Aparna
turns.text: Because you know we don't, this is our only market right now. So as far as rebranding, it would be very easy for us to actually…

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So let me just wrap up mine and you guys can keep going. But ah, look, ah, I’m gonna pass. Lemme tell you why. 2019, very specifically said one thing to investors which is user economics ah matter. Matter very much. And I think you’re great. I think this is a very cool niche business. But as soon as you start going wider and actually start putting marketing money in, one thing you’re going to find about a b2c, you will drink capital marketing this business. This is going to be horrendously expensive to scale. So for that reason, I’m out.
